# How should I size risk?

*You'll need PnL and the position limit (chapter 2), what holding a position costs (chapter 6), a result you can trust
(chapter 11) and the portal's standard error (chapter 12). Written 4 November 2026, before the Arena's rules are
known: everything said here about the Arena is what the organisers had said by then.*

## The story

Qminers' own 2024 hackathon was a sports-betting contest that ended in an in-person final: three rounds, every
finalist's score reset to 1,000 points, a shorter horizon than the qualifier and so more luck in the result. Before
it, the eventual winner wrote a small simulation of the final: the twenty finalists, each with a model of its own
quality and its own appetite for risk, the models correlated with each other (his "Quant factor", after a paper on quant funds that crowded into the
same trades). He used it to choose the fraction of his bankroll to bet, choosing the fraction that won the
final most often, not the one that made most on average
[(`references/qminers-hackathon-2024/README.md:41-49`)]{.src}.

He took the lead in the first round and extended it in the second. Before the third he worked out that its data came
from just after covid, a period other finalists' models might handle better than his, and with a large lead he halved
his stake. It was, in his words, "a minor mistake": his model "performed the best during this time", and at full stake
he estimates he would have ended near 143,000 points. He kept "a dominant first place lead" anyway
[(`references/qminers-hackathon-2024/README.md:55-63`)]{.src}, finishing on 107,074 against the runner-up's 69,460;
two finalists ended under 40 points [(`references/qminers-hackathon-2024/final_scores.png`)]{.src}.

The point is not that halving was right or wrong. It is that he asked a different question from the one a backtest
answers. A backtest asks what makes the most. A final asks what keeps the place.

## The idea

### What the score rewards

How much risk to carry depends first on how the competition turns PnL into a ranking, and competitions differ
[(`references/wiki/concepts/risk-and-protecting-a-lead.md`)]{.src}:

- **Prosperity** ranked teams by cumulative PnL: a large win counts in full, and so does a large loss.
- **UChicago's 2026 competition** scored each round by rank, the square of one less than a team's place among 41,
  the lowest total winning, and weighted the later rounds more
  [(`references/uchicago-trading-2026/README.md:83`, `:221`)]{.src}. A big win counts no more than a narrow one, and a
  bad round costs more the worse it is, so consistency wins.
- **AlgoTrade** scored each round's profit on a log scale against the round's best, and any loss as zero
  [(`references/algotrade2026-pitfa19/.firecrawl/algotrade-participant-guide.md:415-426`)]{.src}. A loss is capped and a
  win only compresses, which makes a long shot cheap.

The Arena, as far as anyone knew on 4 November: its leaderboard ranks each round by PnL, with no total across rounds;
the site's code holds a weighted score over four phases at 10, 20, 30 and 40% that no page uses, so the weights are
the site's and unconfirmed; and whether profit carries from one round to the next is unknown. The Technical Rules,
published at the opening, should settle all three [(`ON_THE_DAY.md`, "Known so far")]{.src}.

### Rank is not expected profit

Under any of these rules, the objective is a place, and a place is a step function of your score against everyone
else's. That changes the sign of risk. A team behind needs a large positive draw to pass the teams ahead, so variance
helps it: the chance of a big enough result rises with the spread, even at the same mean. A team ahead only needs the
others not to pass it, so variance hurts it: every extra unit of spread is a new way to fall. The 2024 winner's
simulation is the general tool, and the repo has one for the last round: `experiments.day.standings` reads the
leaderboards so far, simulates the last round many times, and gives our chance of first, of the top three and of losing
a place for each risk multiplier and each hedge [(`python/experiments/day/standings.py`)]{.src}.

@fig-stake is that calculator on a synthetic field, since there are no Arena leaderboards yet. The field was generated
with 30 teams over three rounds whose medians and spreads were 5, 10 and 20 thousand in the field's units, a team's
skill persisting from round to round at a correlation of 0.7, one common bet worth half a team's variance, and us 3
standard deviations of skill above the field, holding none of the bet. From those leaderboards the calculator measured
what it would measure on real ones: the last round's field with a median of 2,883 and a spread of 23,934, persistence
0.52, the common bet 35% of a team's variance, our loading on it −0.10, and our lead 12,292 points with the rounds
summed at the site's 10, 20, 30 and 40% [(`IDEAS.md`, "A standings calculator for round 4")]{.src}. The last round is simulated 5,000 times, seeded, for three
versions of our last round at full risk: steady (a mean of 35 thousand, a spread of 11), weak (10 and 19) and volatile
(35 and 49). The risk multiplier k scales our round's spread; on the left it scales the mean too, as a smaller position
earns proportionally less, and on the right it leaves the mean alone, as if the risk cut carried no edge
[(`data/standings.csv`; `IDEAS.md`, "A standings calculator for round 4")]{.src}.

![The leader's chance of finishing first against the risk it carries into the last round, in a simulated final: three
kinds of last round, with the edge scaling with the stake (left) or not (right). An illustration of the method on a
synthetic field, not a forecast of the Arena. Data: `data/standings.csv`, from `experiments.day.standings --synthetic
--seed 4 --lead 3`.](../figures/g20_stake.png){#fig-stake
fig-alt="Two line charts of the chance of first against the risk multiplier. Left, where a smaller stake earns proportionally less: every curve rises with the stake; the steady leader goes from 63 percent at a quarter to 94 at full risk and 98 at one and a half; halving costs it 16 points. Right, where a smaller stake keeps its edge: every curve falls; the volatile leader goes from 73 percent at full risk to 86 at half and 93 at a quarter; the steady one barely moves, 94 to 95."}

The two panels give opposite answers, and that is the lesson. If cutting risk cuts the edge with it, a leader with a
good bot should keep its risk: halving the steady bot takes its chance of first from 94% to 78%. If the risk cut is
pure noise, cutting it protects the lead, by a lot for the volatile bot (73% to 86% at half) and hardly at all for the
steady one. Even then, "keep everything" was never far worse for a steady leader. So the question to ask before
halving is not "am I ahead?" but "does the risk I'd remove carry edge?". The 2024 winner removed risk that, as it turned
out, carried his best edge of the final, and gave up about 36,000 points, by his estimate, of a margin he didn't need.

### Kelly: size by edge over odds

The classical answer to "how much of my bankroll" is Kelly's: bet the fraction that maximises the long-run growth of
capital you reinvest. For a bet that wins b units per unit staked with probability p, and loses the stake otherwise,
with q the chance of losing (Thorp, PDF p. 6):

::: {.eq speak="the Kelly fraction is the edge, b times p minus q, the expected gain per unit staked, divided by the odds b"}
$$f^* = \frac{bp - q}{b}$$
:::

On an even-money coin that wins 53% of the time, the fraction is 0.53 less 0.47, or 0.06: bet 6% of what you have on
each flip.
Bet more than about 12% and capital shrinks to nothing despite the edge (Example 2.1, p. 6). Three facts from Thorp
carry over to a trading round, where the formula itself doesn't. **Size follows edge over variance**: in its
continuous form the fraction is the excess drift over the variance (p. 24). **Over-betting is the expensive mistake**:
betting half the optimum keeps three quarters of the growth, and one and a half
times Kelly keeps the same three quarters with three times half Kelly's volatility (p. 26). **Estimated edges are too high**,
through data mining, markets that change and rivals drawn to the same edge, so bet between half and all of the
*estimated* optimum, which protects against negative growth at a likely cost of at most a quarter of it (pp. 29–30).

What doesn't carry is the objective. A round's PnL isn't reinvested, the position limit caps the size where Kelly's
bankroll would, nobody goes broke, and maximising log growth over many bets is not maximising a place over four rounds
[(`references/wiki/sources/kelly-criterion.md`, "Assumptions against the Arena")]{.src}. In a bot, the Kelly-shaped knobs
are the share of the limit a product's quotes use, `make_size`, and its `skew` (chapter 6): a product with a thin edge
and a jumpy price earns a smaller share than one with a fat edge and a quiet price.

Ryan Challman's `ROBOT_DISHES` (chapter 11) is the third fact in practice. Its mean reversion made 96% of its backtest
profit on one of three days (*their claim*). They read the other two days' small profits as noisy estimates of a real
edge, not as noise around zero, and its size on the scored day as unknowable, so they cut its weight from 0.12 to 0.06 rather than size to the best day: shading an estimate they had reason to
think too high [(`references/prosperity4-ryan-challman/README.md:115-141`)]{.src}.

### Value at risk: size the bet to the lead

Kelly sizes against a bankroll; a leader can size against the lead instead. Prosperity 3's runners-up, Frankfurt
Hedgehogs, led every round but the last and came into it 200,000 SeaShells ahead, in the game's currency. Their option mean-reversion strategy
had lost about 50,000 the round before, and they no longer believed in it on its own merits. But several teams close behind traded
only that: if it paid, those teams would close the gap. So they kept some of it, as a hedge against their rivals rather
than against the market. Having decided that, they checked its 95% value at risk, the loss it would exceed only one
time in twenty: about 50,000, "only about 25% of our lead" (*their claim*)
[(`references/prosperity3-frankfurt-hedgehogs/README.md:616`)]{.src}. Turned around, their check is a sizing rule, our
generalisation rather than theirs:

::: {.eq speak="size the bet so that its ninety-five percent value at risk is at most a set share s of the lead; Frankfurt Hedgehogs' check came out at s equal to a quarter"}
$$\text{VaR}_{95\%}(\text{the bet}) \le s \times \text{lead}, \qquad s = \tfrac{1}{4}\ \text{in Frankfurt Hedgehogs' check}$$
:::

In that round, about 190,000 ahead of the second team, they also half-hedged their baskets and limited mean
reversion, to play it safe [(`references/prosperity3-frankfurt-hedgehogs/README.md:759`)]{.src}. They kept a healthy distance to
every team that had been close behind, the ones they had hedged against, and still finished second: a team from below
100th place made about 850,000 in the last round, against the 200,000 to 400,000 typical of the top teams, and took
first [(`references/prosperity3-frankfurt-hedgehogs/README.md:3`, `:616`, `:765-769`)]{.src}. A relative hedge protects
against the rivals you can see, not against a long shot that comes off. The standings calculator's hedge
table prices the same idea: the share of the field's common bet to hold so that a swing can't reorder the ranks. On
the synthetic field, holding half to all of it cut the steady leader's chance of losing a place from 6% to 4%
[(`IDEAS.md`, "A standings calculator for round 4")]{.src}. Small insurance, with the bet free
to hold; on a field that isn't all in on one bet, there is nothing to hedge.

### The tail you can't backtest

The cleanest case for sizing a risk to zero is one the backtest never shows. The winners of UChicago's 2026 Case 1 click-traded
prediction markets by hand, from a physical DJ deck, on top of their algorithm. The exchange froze sporadically, and in
round 6 it froze while they held large positions and news hit: about $200,000 gone in seconds, a top-5 round turned
into 35th. They stopped trading by hand for the remaining six rounds, and wrote afterwards that, given a leaderboard
that rewarded consistent placing, they should never have started. In the last round they computed that the top 11 of
41 was enough for first overall and stopped their bot after about 8 minutes, while other teams were manipulating the
books in the final minutes (*their claim*)
[(`references/uchicago-trading-2026/README.md:197-203`, `:227-233`)]{.src}.

Two habits come out of it. Size a risk by what it can lose in its worst minute, not by its average contribution: a
side bet whose expected gain is small and whose tail is large is negative under any rank-based score. And know, before
the last round, what result is enough. In the repo, the per-product loss stop is the bot's own version of the first:
`stop_loss` flattens a product and stops it for the day once its PnL falls that far below its high, sized from
`arena.stress` at about three times its plain drawdown [(`RUNBOOK.md`, "Each round", T+1:30; `IDEAS.md`, "A loss stop per product")]{.src}.

### Round weights and carry-over

How the four rounds combine decides how much a round's lead is worth, and the day's question file works through each
case [(`ON_THE_DAY.md`, "How is PnL scored?")]{.src}. If the total is a weighted sum of raw PnL, a lead counts in its own
round's units, and round 1, a simple market while most teams are still learning the API, may be where a prepared team's
lead is largest, so even at 10% it can matter as much as later rounds. If rounds are normalised or ranked, a big win
counts little more than a narrow one. If profit carries over into the next round's capital, an early gain compounds and
an early loss shrinks every later round, as in Qminers' 2024 and 2025 contests
[(`IDEAS.md`, "Round 1 as the prepared team's largest PnL lead")]{.src}.

So RUNBOOK leaves the decision to the one point where the information exists: before round 4, decide in writing how
much risk to keep, and any relative hedge, from the standings calculator run on the three real leaderboards, our rank
under each way the rounds may combine; and if rounds 2 and 3's private runs strayed from our backtests, a bot that sends
nothing goes on the list [(`RUNBOOK.md`, "Rules that hold all day")]{.src}. Zero is a candidate, as a model that
abstains is a candidate in a selective-prediction task.

::: {.callout-note title="What would differ on another market"}
On Prosperity, where the ranking was cumulative PnL, Frankfurt Hedgehogs sized
their hedge in the game's currency against a lead in the same. Under UChicago's squared ranks, the same lead is worth nothing once
first place is safe, so stopping was right. On AlgoTrade, with losses scored as zero, a trailing team's long shot cost
little. The Qminers 2024 final compounded a bankroll, where Kelly's own objective almost applies. The Arena's rule
picks among these, and none of the numbers above is a fact about it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
A competition ranked on one final evaluation rewards the probability of finishing first, not the expected score, the
way a Kaggle private leaderboard rewards robustness over the public score; the standings calculator is a Monte Carlo
over the field, exactly as you would simulate a leaderboard shake-up. Where the analogy breaks: on Kaggle you choose the
model once, before the private score exists. Here the stake can change from round to round after you have seen the
standings, so the choice of risk is itself a sequential decision on new information, and the rivals are making it too.
:::
